newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition united on income tax cuts - paper.
newsitem.headline: German coalition united on income tax cuts - paper.

text.p: Leaders of Germany's governing coalition have reached agreement on how much to cut income tax as part of a major fiscal reform in 1999, the Bild newspaper's Sunday edition reported.

A coalition tax commission headed by Finance Minister Theo Waigel has agreed on lowering the lowest tax bracket to 20 percent from 25.9 percent. The top rate should fall to 40 percent from 53 percent now, Bild am Sonntag said.
Other news reports said, however, that the tax commission had still not ironed out its differences and would not be able to present a final proposal when it meets next Wednesday.
A finance ministry spokeswoman confirmed that it could be January before the plan is finalised, but added slight delays were unimportant in a project of such scope.
"There is no question of the commission being divided -- the negotiating climate is constructive," she told Reuters.
Germany is working to overhaul its complex and increasingly inefficient tax system to meet and stick to the tight fiscal constraints required under European monetary union, which is planned in 1999.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government also wants to cut the overall tax burden to boost growth and employment in a country where the economic shock arising from unificiation in 1990 has turned west's post-war economic "miracle" into a fading memory.

The tax cuts would knock 80 billion marks off revenues, but that would be partly offset by scrapping 50 billion marks of tax breaks, Bild said. A hike in value-added tax -- which at 15 percent is low by European standards -- is also on the cards.
-- Night, Sunday and holiday work would be liable for tax.
-- Tax writeoffs on property and ships would be scrapped.
-- Benefits, like unemployment pay and pensions, would be tax liable.
-- Car tax would be replaced by an hike in petrol taxes.
Waigel had wanted a cut in the top tax band to 35 percent, but that is now likely only to take place after the year 2000, Bild said, quoting commission sources.
One key outstanding issue is over calls by junior coalition partners the Free Democrats for a three-band income tax system to replace the current sliding scale, Welt am Sonntag said.
But the newspaper said that the band system was being taken seriously by Waigel and Wolfgang Schaeuble, the powerful parliamentary chief of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).
